slides.title: Reference Material As A Model Shelf
slides.notes: Open the appendix as a shelf of models that the main course repeatedly borrows from. The point is not to teach an entire topology course, but to make four tools operational: loop invariants, cohomology ledgers, hyperbolic models, and reproducible programming scaffolds.

slides.title: Fundamental Groups Remember Loop Failure
slides.notes: Use the basepoint as the anchor that turns loops into algebra. The diagram separates the moving curve from its endpoint-fixed class, then shows why concatenation becomes multiplication. Stress that the reference material supplies a reusable diagnostic, not a catalog of all possible spaces.

slides.title: Covering Spaces Turn Loops Into Actions
slides.notes: Explain the cover as a machine for unwrapping loops. A closed path downstairs can lift to a path whose endpoint has moved upstairs, and that shift is exactly the kind of group action geometric group theory likes to inspect. The integer labels are bookkeeping for deck translations.

slides.title: Group Cohomology Is A Quotient Ledger
slides.notes: Present cohomology as algebraic accounting. Cochains record candidate data, cocycles satisfy a compatibility equation, and coboundaries are changes of coordinates or harmless rewrites. The quotient keeps what cannot be removed, which is why cohomology is useful for extensions and obstruction language.

slides.title: A Cocycle Measures Failed Multiplication
slides.notes: This slide gives a concrete reason cohomology belongs in a geometric group theory appendix. A chosen section of an extension may not preserve multiplication, and the visible triangular defect records that failure. Changing the section changes representatives, while the cohomology class preserves the obstruction.

slides.title: Hyperbolic Plane Models Require Conventions
slides.notes: Slow down on model choice. The disk and half-plane are both valid windows into the same hyperbolic plane, but their Euclidean appearances can mislead students. Boundary points are infinitely far away in the metric, and geodesics are determined by model-specific rules.

slides.title: Disk Geodesics And Distance Checks
slides.notes: Connect the generated appendix artifacts to mathematical sanity checks. Orthogonal arcs and diameters are the visual grammar of disk geodesics, while the distance formula supplies immediate tests: symmetry, positivity, and boundary growth. Those tests are deliberately small enough to audit after reruns.

slides.title: Programming Tasks Need A Proof-Aware Scaffold
slides.notes: Frame programming tasks as experiments with responsibilities. Before code, name the object and predicted invariant. During computation, keep the model small enough to inspect. Afterward, save an artifact and a check so the result remains teachable outside the live notebook.

slides.title: Reference Tools Reappear Across The Course
slides.notes: Use the routing map to tie the appendix back to earlier chapters. Fundamental groups enter through covers and actions, cohomology organizes obstruction language, hyperbolic models clarify negative curvature, and programming scaffolds keep each finite window honest about what it can and cannot prove.

slides.title: Appendix Exit Checklist
slides.notes: Close with an instructor checklist rather than another theorem. For any borrowed reference tool, students should identify the invariant, the model convention, the saved artifact, and the sanity check. That habit keeps the appendix active throughout the course instead of becoming background reading.
